info.bio:
Músico de Florida de la década de los 60 que se inicia tras formar parte de grupos juveniles con la International Submarine Band, primer grupo que fusiona el country rock.  A finales de esa década se une a los Byrds y después a Chris Hilmann para formar Flyng Burrito Brothers el gran grupo del country rock. En sus últimos discos se hace acompañar por Emmylou Harris.
Fallece trágicamente y sus amigos se llevan su cadáver para enterrarle en el desierto.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

podcast.title: Death and Desert Cremation (September 19, 1973)
podcast.body: Graham Parsons, former member of The Byrds, died of an overdose at age 26 on September 19, 1973, in room 8 at the Joshua Tree Inn in California. His body was then spirited away by his road manager from LAX to be cremated in the desert in a private ritual. A pile of stones known as Cap Rock is believed to be where the cremation took place. "This is where Graham Parsons, ex of the birds, died of an overdose at age 26 on September 19th, 1973."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death and Body Snatching
podcast.body: Parsons died on September 19, 1973, from a drug overdose, embodying a "true 70s rock star fashion." He had expressed a wish to be cremated and have his remains scattered in the Joshua Tree desert, contrary to his family's desire for a burial in Louisiana. His manager, Phil Kaufman, stole Parsons' body from Los Angeles International Airport and performed a DIY cremation in the desert, an event that significantly contributed to his legend and popularity. "He died on September 19th 1973 in true 70s rock star fashion of a drug overdose."

podcast.title: Dislike for "Country Rock" Label
podcast.body: Parsons strongly disliked the term "country rock" to categorize his music, famously referring to it as "a plastic dry fuck." He preferred his own descriptive, "cosmic American music," which better encompassed his broad artistic vision. "Parsons, no surprise, did not like the term country rock, which he referred to as, and I shall quote, a plastic dry fuck."

podcast.title: Founding the International Submarine Band
podcast.body: While a student at Harvard, Parsons co-founded the International Submarine Band with John Nuese, which is widely considered one of the earliest country rock groups, regardless of Parsons' personal dislike for the genre label. "Parsons and John News formed what many considered to be one of the earliest country rock bands, whether Graham liked the term or not, called the International Submarine Band."

podcast.title: Influence on Youth and Country Music
podcast.body: Gram Parsons is noted for making country music "cool for younger people to like," an influence shared, and perhaps even surpassed, by Linda Ronstadt. "We know that she may be even more than Grand Parsons made it cool for younger people to like country music."

podcast.title: Musical Chemistry with Emmylou Harris
podcast.body: Gram Parsons shared a unique and profound "musical chemistry" with Emmylou Harris, creating a "gorgeous duet partnership" that many consider unparalleled. Their strong emotional and possibly spiritual connection was evident in their collaborations, despite Parsons being married during their time together. "I'm not sure if there has ever been or ever will be a duet partnership that is as gorgeous as the one between Graham and Emileu."

podcast.title: Musical Influences and "Cosmic American Music"
podcast.body: Parsons was deeply influenced by diverse American musical forms, including gospel, Elvis's early country-tinged rock, and particularly Ray Charles' 1965 album "Country and Western Meets Rhythm and Blues." He coined the term "cosmic American music" to describe his fusion of all types of American music, intentionally crossing genre and cultural boundaries, defining it as a "stew." "He said it's cosmic American music."

podcast.title: Nudie Suits and Image
podcast.body: Parsons was known for his distinctive "nudie suits," which were custom-tailored and often featured elaborate designs. His specific suit included marijuana leaves, poppy flowers, and naked ladies on the lapel, reflecting a "psychedelic cow punk" image that contributed to his legendary status. "Graham suit with its marijuana leaves and poppy flowers. He's got these naked ladies on the lapel. It's definitely one of a kind."

podcast.title: Pioneer of Country Rock
podcast.body: Gram Parsons, through his band The Flying Burrito Brothers, was instrumental in establishing the country rock style that became popular in the 1970s and influenced bands like the early Eagles. "She worked really closely with Graham Parsons whose flying burrito brothers band really set the stage for the country rock style that was so popular in the 70s you know think early Eagles."

podcast.title: Trust Fund Background
podcast.body: Gram Parsons was a privileged white individual who received a significant annual income of $55,000 from a trust fund, stemming from his grandfather's Florida Citrus Empire. This financial independence meant he never had to worry about money, a fact that some critics argued placed him outside the "struggle" often considered an essential element of authentic country music. "He was a privileged white kid who lived off the 55,000 or whatever it was, a year that he got from his trust fund."
